title: Benchmarking semantic code retrieval on Claude Code — Kuba Rogut, Turbopuffer

primary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is semantic code retrieval using vector search, embeddings, and chunking strategies for AI coding agents. The benchmarked systems (Claude Code, Cursor) are coding assistants, and the core subject is search and retrieval within codebases. The talk evaluates production coding agents using a benchmark methodology (ContextBench) across 50 tasks. Requires familiarity with vector search, embeddings, precision/recall metrics, and coding agent architectures. Conference presentation with video demos and Q&A from the AI Engineer channel. Provides quantitative benchmark results with specific precision, recall, retention, and satisfaction metrics.

summary: Kuba Rogut from Turbopuffer presents a benchmark study on adding semantic code retrieval to Claude Code. Turbopuffer is a serverless full-text and vector search database built on object storage, serving companies like Cursor, Anthropic, and Notion. Early Claude Code versions used a local vector DB for semantic search but switched to agentic search (grepping) because it worked better and was simpler. However, Cursor—Turbopuffer's first customer—indexes codebases into Turbopuffer and reports real gains: 24% relative improvement in answer accuracy with their composer model, 12.5-13% across all models, 2.6% increase in code retention in large codebases, and 2.2% decrease in dissatisfied user requests. These numbers appear small because not every query benefits from semantic search. Kuba frames embeddings as cache compute: agentic search repeats grep/read cycles every session, while semantic search incurs upfront chunking and indexing costs but caches semantic meaning for faster, cheaper subsequent queries. He built Turbo Grep, a CLI tool using a tree splitter to chunk codebases, embed with the Voyage code 3 model, and upload to Turbopuffer. The benchmark uses ContextBench, a public human-labeled dataset testing whether agents find the right files, lines, and symbols—not just whether they solved the problem. Three conditions were tested across 50 tasks: raw Claude Code, 50-line windowed reads, and windowed reads plus Turbopuffer semantic search. File precision rose from 65% baseline to 87% with semantic search; wasted reads dropped from 1 in 3 to 1 in 8. Semantic search excelled on behavior-adjacent tasks where files share no keywords; grep won on import tracing where keywords are present. Kuba's gains were smaller than Cursor's because Claude Code treats semantic search as just another tool, whereas Cursor's composer is trained to know when and why to use it. In Q&A, Kuba clarified semantic search here is simple vector search on raw code chunks, but noted sophisticated customers like Cursor go further—injecting synthetic comments into code before embedding to boost recall. He observed semantic search works best on well-commented code with inline documentation. He also emphasized vector DBs are built for multiplayer, complex relationships, and multimodal data (video, audio, images) that grep cannot handle, and that tools shrinking billion-token context windows to the right million will win long-term.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Turbopuffer background
sections.summary: Kuba introduces himself and Turbopuffer, a serverless full-text and vector search database built on object storage serving fast-growing AI companies.

sections.title: Claude Code's default search and Cursor's semantic search gains
sections.summary: Claude Code defaults to agentic grep-based search; early versions tried a local vector DB but found grep simpler. Cursor, Turbopuffer's first customer, indexes codebases and reports 24% composer accuracy improvement, 2.6% code retention increase, and 2.2% fewer dissatisfied requests. Numbers look small because not every query benefits from semantic search.

sections.title: Embeddings as cache compute
sections.summary: Frames embeddings as cached compute: agentic search repeats grep/read cycles every session while semantic search pays upfront indexing costs then reuses cached semantic meaning for faster, cheaper queries, especially when running multiple agents simultaneously.

sections.title: Turbo Grep CLI tool
sections.summary: Built a simple CLI tool called Turbo Grep that uses a tree splitter to chunk codebases, embeds with the Voyage code model, and uploads to Turbopuffer. Includes a demo video showing Claude Code calling the T Puffer search tool in the Django repo.

sections.title: ContextBench methodology and three test conditions
sections.summary: ContextBench is a human-labeled benchmark testing whether agents find the right files, lines, and symbols during problem-solving. Three conditions tested: raw Claude Code, 50-line windowed reads, and windowed reads plus Turbopuffer semantic search. The 50-line cap reduces noise from full-file reads.

sections.title: Precision results
sections.summary: File precision rose from 65% baseline to 87% with semantic search. In human terms: wasted reads dropped from 1 in 3 (raw) to 1 in 5 (windowed grep) to 1 in 8 (semantic search). Claude Code's exploratory nature shows in the 65% baseline.

sections.title: Recall results and task-type breakdown
sections.summary: Claude Code wins file recall by default due to exhaustive exploration, but line recall drops as it reads many irrelevant files. Semantic search won on behavior-adjacent tasks where files share no keywords (e.g., different ORMs across libraries); grep won on import tracing where keywords are directly present.

sections.title: Summary and comparison to Cursor
sections.summary: Semantic search boosted precision significantly. Gains were smaller than Cursor's because Claude Code is built for grepping and treats semantic search as an extra tool, while Cursor's composer is trained to know when and how to use it. Long-term, lightweight tools that find context in various ways will win.

sections.title: Q&A: Semantic search definition, comments, and Cursor's approach
sections.summary: Kuba defines semantic search as simple vector search using Voyage code 3 embeddings sent to Turbopuffer. Semantic search works best on well-commented code with inline documentation because comments give the embedding model richer semantic meaning. His benchmark used only raw code chunks, but sophisticated customers like Cursor inject synthetic comments into code before embedding to boost recall. Cursor also has its own embedding model that translates code into human-level queries.

sections.title: Q&A: Vector DB use cases beyond grep
sections.summary: Kuba explains vector DBs are built for multiplayer, complex data relationships, and multimodal data (video, audio, images) that grep cannot handle. Examples include Notion knowledge bases and multimodal content. Grep remains valuable for zero-cost local file system search, but at scale or with complex/multimodal data, vector DBs help cache semantic meaning for agents.
